query: For refractory high-entropy alloys intended for jet-turbine applications, what single intervention could improve high-temperature mechanical capability while limiting density and preserving room-temperature performance? Formulate one hypothesis that specifies the intervention, its mechanism, the expected improvement relative to a relevant baseline, the temperature and loading conditions under which it should hold, supporting evidence from prior studies, and a decisive experiment with a result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Partially substituting heavier refractory elements (e.g., W or Ta) with a small atomic fraction (2–5 at.%) of aluminum in a baseline refractory high-entropy alloy will reduce alloy density, promote a beneficial B2 precipitate fraction that strengthens the alloy at elevated temperatures, and preserve at least 80–90% of its baseline room-temperature strength and ductility.
generation.material_initial_state: An as-cast NbMoTaW or similarly dense Refractory High-Entropy Alloy (RHEA) with a predominantly single-phase BCC microstructure, melted and homogenized under vacuum or inert atmosphere.
generation.intervention: Replace 2–5 at.% of the heaviest refractory constituent (e.g., W or Ta) with Al, followed by standard homogenization heat treatment to stabilize the microstructure.
generation.conditions: Test mechanical performance in tension or uniaxial compression from room temperature up to ~1200 °C (jet-turbine operating range). Monitor density and measure yield strength, ultimate tensile/compressive strength, and ductility at both ambient and elevated temperatures.
generation.structural_mediator: Formation of stable B2 precipitates (containing Al and refractory elements), which enhance high-temperature strength via precipitation strengthening mechanisms and maintain sufficient lattice distortions at room temperature for ductility.
generation.mechanism: Al atoms lower the overall atomic mass and partially stabilize a B2 phase that resists dislocation motion at elevated temperatures, thereby improving high-temperature strength without severely embrittling the alloy at room temperature.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the baseline alloy, the Al-substituted RHEA will exhibit (1) ~3–5% lower density, (2) ~10–15% higher yield strength at ~1200 °C, and (3) minimal (≤10–20%) degradation of room-temperature ductility and strength.
generation.baseline: Unmodified NbMoTaW or a similar dense Mo/Ta/W-based RHEA without Al doping, processed under analogous melting and homogenization conditions.
generation.boundary: Above ~5 at.% Al, excessive B2 or other brittle intermetallic formation may compromise room-temperature ductility. The final microstructure’s phase stability and composition homogeneity must remain within design ranges for the hypothesized benefit.
generation.uncertainty: If the alloy undergoes unanticipated phase formation (e.g., brittle intermetallics) or if Al does not partition effectively to form stable B2 precipitates, then high-temperature performance or ductility may fall below predictions.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two series of NbMoTaW-based alloys, one baseline (no Al) and one with 2–5 at.% Al added in place of W or Ta. Homogenize both sets identically. Conduct high-temperature tensile or compressive tests at increments up to ~1200 °C; also measure room-temperature strength and ductility. Compare density measurements using Archimedean or X-ray density techniques.
measurements: Tensile or compressive strength and elongation/strain-to-failure at room temperature and at ~1200 °C
Microstructural analysis (SEM/TEM) to identify phases (BCC, B2, and any other precipitates)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Al-doped alloys fail to demonstrate an increased yield strength relative to the baseline alloy at high temperature (1200 °C) or if the room-temperature ductility declines by more than 20% compared to baseline, the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: High-entropy alloys (HEAs) are potential engineering materials for demanding applications where exceptional damage tolerance, good wear, high oxidation and corrosion resistance is needed,. Although HEAs are composed of several equimolar or near equimolar elements, their solid solution phases often are face-centered cubic (fcc), hexagonal close packed (hcp) or bcc. As novel high-temperature structural and functional materials, HEAs consisting of refractory metallic elements (Ti, Zr, Hf, V, Nb, Ta, Cr, Mo, and W) are single bcc phase and have been in the focus of several experimental studies,,,,,,,,,. High strength and good ductility are essential demands on the mechanical performance of structural materials. Some refractory HEAs with disordered bcc solid solution phase,, such as CrNbTiZr and CrNbTiVZr, were found to exhibit high compressive yield strength up to 1.3 GPa. The observed low ductility at room temperature limits, however, their potential application. The tensile strength of refractory HEAs has hardly been investigated. Refractory high-entropy alloys (RHEAs) are a relatively new class of multicomponent materials that are based on several refractory metals, but may also contain other, generally low density, elements and typically have a body centered cubic (BCC) crystal structure. These alloys have recently received much attention because of their attractive combination of properties not achievable by other classes of metallic alloys. For example, the first two RHEAs, NbMoTaW and NbMoTaVW, showed weak temperature dependence of yield strength in the temperature range from 600 °C to 1600 °C, with yield strength above 400 MPa at 1600 °C,. Unfortunately, these two alloys had high density (>12 g/cm3) and further developments aimed at reducing the alloy density while keeping superior high-temperature properties. In the second generation RHEAs, high-density Ta and W were replaced with lower density refractory elements, such as Cr, Mo, Nb, V and Zr, and low density Al and Ti were added. This resulted in RHEAs with lower densities and high-temperature strengths better than the properties of Ni-based superalloys and Fe-based steels.
